pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s the big idea is that the brain is the body's CONTROL CENTRE, sitting protected inside the skull, running a constant loop: the senses send it information, it thinks and decides, and it sends messages out through nerves to tell muscles what to do. The single most teachable thing is this SENSE → BRAIN → MUSCLE loop, made concrete with a vivid everyday example (eyes see a ball coming → brain decides 'catch!' → nerves tell the hands to move). Children this age tend to think of the brain vaguely as 'where thinking happens' and don't connect it to movement or the senses; the goal is to make the brain the hub that receives, decides, and commands. Keep it to the loop and the control-centre idea — no neurons, lobes or chemistry — and let children generate their own examples (catching, flinching, answering a question) so the loop is recognised in their own actions.
bestPractices: Teach the SENSE → BRAIN → MUSCLE loop as the organising idea, always with a concrete action (catch a ball, pull hand from something hot), so the brain is linked to movement, not just thinking.

Have children generate their own examples and act them out, tracing 'what did your senses tell your brain? what did your brain decide? what did it tell your muscles?' — turning the loop into a body activity.
Locate and protect: the brain is inside the skull (feel your head), which keeps this control centre safe — a simple structure–function point.
Use the messages-in / messages-out framing (nerves as the body's wires) to prepare the later nervous-system topic without naming parts.
Avoid over-detail (neurons, brain regions); keep the brain a single 'boss' that receives, decides and commands.
keyRepresentations: The SENSE → BRAIN → MUSCLE loop drawn as a simple three-step cycle
A worked everyday example (ball → eyes → brain 'catch!' → hands) acted out
The brain as the body's 'control centre / boss' sending and receiving messages
Nerves shown as message-carrying wires between brain and body
Skull-as-helmet protecting the brain (feel your head)
commonMisconceptions: 'The brain is only for thinking/schoolwork' — missing that it also controls movement and receives all the senses.
'The heart controls the body / feelings come from the heart' — a common young-child idea; the brain is the control centre.
'Muscles move by themselves' — missing that the brain sends the command through nerves.
'The senses work on their own' — not connecting that senses report TO the brain, which then decides.
'The brain and body are separate' — not seeing the constant two-way messaging between them.
'You have to think about everything you do' — (gently) some responses are very fast/automatic, previewing reflexes later.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach the brain as the body's CONTROL CENTRE through a repeatable SENSE → BRAIN → MUSCLE loop: the senses send information in, the brain decides, and messages travel out through nerves to tell muscles what to do. Anchor it in a vivid everyday action (eyes see a ball → brain decides 'catch!' → nerves tell the hands to move), and let children generate and act out their own examples so they recognise the same loop in their own catching, turning, and answering. Keep it to the loop and the control-centre idea — no neurons, lobes, or chemistry. Confront the common ideas that the brain is only for thinking, that the heart does the deciding, and that muscles move by themselves.

activities.title: Trigger the loop: sense in, brain decides, muscle out
feedback: If a learner says the hands catch by themselves, replay the step where the brain sends the message DOWN to the hands and ask: 'What told the hands the moment to close?'
If a learner only describes the brain 'seeing', prompt both ends: 'What sent the message IN to the brain? What message went OUT to the muscles?'
When a learner narrates both the sense-in and the message-out correctly, affirm: 'Yes — the brain took in what your eyes reported and then commanded your hands.'
Compare two scenarios: 'The ball used your eyes and the tap on your shoulder used your skin — but what three steps did BOTH have?'
activities.rationale: The concept is itself a loop of information flow, which young children are asked to capture with a model. Letting the child trigger a stimulus and watch the messages fire makes the loop causal and repeatable; routing the same loop through different senses and muscles is what reveals the brain as a general control hub rather than a thing that only 'thinks'. A live animation is proposed because it can show the message travelling over time, which a single still image does not depict; both media can teach the loop, and this is a design proposal, not a proven comparison.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-LS1-2] (taught with a model at the elementary level).
The nervous system, with the brain as the control centre, coordinates the body by receiving sensory information and directing responses through nerves to muscles.
learnerActions: Choose a situation: a ball flying at you, someone tapping your shoulder, or a friend calling your name.
Start the scene and watch a message light up FROM the sense (eyes, skin, or ears) and race up to the brain.

Watch the brain show a quick 'decide' beat (a little thought bubble), then fire a command DOWN to the right muscles so the character acts — catches the ball, turns to see who tapped, or turns round to answer.
Run a slow-motion replay and narrate each step out loud: 'my eyes told my brain, my brain decided, my brain told my hands.'
Try all three scenarios and notice what stays the same and what changes.
activities.intendedInsight: The SAME three-step loop — sense in, brain decides, muscle out — runs every time, just through different senses and body parts, so the brain is the control centre that wires the whole body together.

activities.title: Act out your own loop
feedback: If a learner skips the sense step, ask: 'Which part of your body noticed first — your eyes, ears, or skin?'
If a learner skips the muscle step, ask: 'Which muscles moved, and who told them to?'
Praise examples that correctly identify a different starting sense: 'Good — this one started with your ears, not your eyes, but the brain still decided.'
activities.rationale: Having children generate and physically perform their own examples turns the loop into a body activity and helps them recognise it in their own behaviour, which may support transfer beyond the single ball example. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-LS1-2] (taught with a model at the elementary level).
learnerActions: Think of something YOU do: catching a ball, scratching when you feel an itch, turning when someone calls your name, or answering a question.
Act it out with your body.
Trace it aloud: 'What did my senses tell my brain? What did my brain decide? What did my brain tell my muscles?'
Do a second example that starts with a different sense (hearing, touch, sight).
activities.intendedInsight: The loop isn't just in a model — it runs in the child's own deliberate actions, through whichever sense started it.

activities.title: Feel the helmet: where the brain sits
feedback: If a learner says the brain is 'only for thinking', give a movement or posture example: 'Right now your brain is keeping you upright — that's a job too.'
Affirm the structure–function point: 'The skull is like a helmet that protects the boss of your body.'
activities.rationale: A simple locate-and-protect observation grounds the abstract control-centre idea in the child's own body and gently broadens the brain's role beyond schoolwork thinking. No cited source directly supports the skull-protection point; it rests on the pedagogy summary.
learnerActions: Feel the hard bone of your skull with your hands.
Talk about why the brain — the body's control centre — is kept inside something hard and strong.
Name one job the brain is doing right now that isn't 'thinking hard', such as keeping you sitting upright.
activities.intendedInsight: The brain sits protected inside the skull, which keeps this control centre safe — a simple link between structure and function — and it is busy controlling the body even when you aren't thinking hard.

activities.title: Name the parts of the loop (labelling companion)
feedback: If the order is wrong, ask: 'What has to happen FIRST — can your hand move before your brain knows the ball is coming?'
If a scenario is matched to the wrong sense, ask: 'How did you first notice it — did you see it, hear it, or feel it?'
Confirm correct sequences by naming the full chain back to the learner.
activities.rationale: Labelling and sequencing checks the order and vocabulary of the loop. On its own this names parts and checks recognition rather than eliciting the child's own causal narration of messages travelling, so it works best as a companion to the active model, not as the main activity.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-LS1-2] (taught with a model at the elementary level).
learnerActions: On a labelled body, tap the eyes, the brain, the nerves, and a hand muscle to reveal each one's role.
Lift a flap at each step to see 'what message is being sent?'
Put the three steps in order: sense → brain → muscle.
Match a scenario (ball, tap on the shoulder, name called) to the sense that starts it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each part of the loop has a role — the sense reports in, the nerves carry the messages, the brain decides, the muscle acts — and the steps happen in a fixed order.

constraints: Keep to the loop and the control-centre idea only — do not introduce neurons, brain regions, or chemistry at this age.
Treat the brain as a single 'boss' that receives, decides, and commands; the point is the two-way messaging between brain and body, not anatomical detail.
Labelling, sequencing, and matching tasks check recognition and order; they do not require the child to independently narrate the causal chain, so pair them with the active model or acting-out task.
A 'meet your brain, the boss' character could name the control-centre role, but for this age the loop is better shown by acting it out than discussed; keep any persona optional and secondary.

Introduce automatic/fast responses (like keeping upright, or snatching a hand away from something hot, which can happen before the brain has 'decided') only gently as a preview of reflexes; do not overstate it as a full topic, and do not use them as examples of the brain deciding.

The live-animation and slow-motion replay are design suggestions to make the message-travel visible over time; they are not claimed to be the only way to teach this loop, and a static labelled image can still teach the parts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS claim cited is pitched at Grade 4 (4-LS1-2), while this topic targets ages 5–7; the underlying sense→process→respond idea is age-appropriate here, but the specific standard is for older learners. Reviewers may wish to confirm the age mapping.
One source (Britannica overview) is marked unverified in the original row; its claim is used only to support the general control-centre framing, not any efficacy claim.

The original row asserts '3D adds cost with no gain' for this concept; this has been dropped as a universal claim. A spatial model is simply not the focus here (the concept is information flow), which does not establish that 3D teaches nothing.
The original 'quiz only... doesn't build the causal intuition' framing has been softened to a scoped limit: recognition/sequencing tasks do not elicit independent causal narration.

The original artefact note said an animation does what a static picture 'can't'; this has been narrowed to a time-based affordance (showing travel over time) while retaining the static labelled image as a valid teaching companion.
The 'Feel the helmet' activity's skull-protection point is not directly backed by any cited source claim, so its sourceClaims is []; it relies on the pedagogy summary rather than a verified source.
The NGSS claim is reused on activities 2 and 4 to support the loop content taught via a model; the specific pedagogic efficacy of those designs is unproven and they remain proposals.

probeDeeper: How does your hand KNOW the moment to close around the ball? Where did that instruction come from?
If you shut your eyes just as the ball arrived, why would it be much harder to catch — what information would the brain be missing?
Name something your brain is doing for you right now that isn't 'thinking hard' — like keeping you sitting upright.
assess.correctAnswer: The eyes see the ball coming and send that information to the brain; the brain — the control centre in your skull — works out where the ball is going and decides to catch it, then sends messages through nerves to the hand muscles telling them to move to the right place. So the brain isn't just for thinking about schoolwork — it takes in what the senses report and controls the body's movements too.

errorPatterns.pattern: The brain is only for thinking or learning, not for seeing or moving the body.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden the brain's job: it also receives from the senses and commands the muscles; give movement examples, not just 'thinking'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Your hands catch it on their own — the brain is only for thinking about things.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes the brain from movement and senses; says the hands act on their own.

errorPatterns.pattern: You think and feel and decide with your heart, not your brain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the everyday 'heart' of feelings from the organ; the brain is the body's control and decision centre.
errorPatterns.distractor: Your heart decides to catch the ball.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the heart as the decider or thinker.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles move by themselves without any message from the brain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that muscles wait for a message carried by nerves from the brain before they move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the hands moving with no brain-to-muscle instruction.

responseLevels.gap: Says hands catch by themselves, or that thinking and feeling happen in the heart; the brain isn't linked to senses or movement.
responseLevels.full: Describes the full loop — senses send information in, the brain decides, messages go out to the muscles — with a correct example, recognising the brain controls movement and senses, not just thoughts.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the brain is the control centre and thinks, but describes only part of the loop — e.g. the brain sees, without the sense-in or the message-out to the muscles.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you catch a ball someone throws to you, your eyes, your brain, and your hands are all involved. What is your brain's job in catching it, and how does it know to tell your hands to move? Walk me through what happens.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the hands catch by themselves, or that thinking happens in the heart, misses the brain's control role. Only a child who describes information in from the eyes and messages out to the muscles has the loop. The tier-two 'how does it know to tell your hands' forces the sense-in/message-out link.
